mcq.q: Which task is a small model most likely to handle as well as a large one?
options: Answering open questions on rare topics
Writing new code across a large codebase
Planning a multi-step research project
Routing messages into twelve fixed queues
mcq.why: A fixed label set with many examples suits small models.
distractors: Rare topics need knowledge small models lack.
Large code changes need broad knowledge.

mcq.q: A large model costs 0.004 dollars per message at 1 million messages a month. Its monthly cost is…
options: 4 dollars
4,000 dollars
40,000 dollars
400 dollars

mcq.q: The fairest baseline for judging a small model is…
options: A large model with your best prompt, same test set
The small model’s own training accuracy
Published benchmark scores for both
A large model with a minimal prompt
mcq.why: Compare against the strongest simple alternative on your own held-out data.
distractors: Benchmarks may not match your task.
A weak prompt flatters the small model.

mcq.q: Accuracy falls from 95% to 94% on 1 million messages a month. How many more errors a month?
A team switches to a small model because it is 1 point worse overall. Users of one rare queue complain. What did they skip?
options: Quantising the small model
Checking accuracy per slice
Training on more common cases
Measuring the cost difference
mcq.why: Averages hide slices where the small model is much worse.
distractors: More common cases do not help the rare queue.
Cost was the reason for switching.

mcq.q: At 10,000 requests a month, why might a hosted large model be cheaper overall?
options: Small models cost more per token than hosted ones
Training, serving and upkeep of a small model cost more
Small models need larger GPUs than hosted models use
Hosted models are free below a monthly threshold
mcq.why: At low volume the fixed costs of owning a model dominate (13.1).

mcq.q: Which hidden cost comes with a small self-trained model?
options: Losing access when a provider changes terms
Waiting for the provider’s rate limits
Paying per token to the provider
Retraining and monitoring as inputs drift
mcq.why: You own its upkeep (18.6).
distractors: A hosted risk, not a self-trained one.

mcq.q: A small model answers in 20 ms and a large one in 900 ms. For a type-ahead feature, the latency difference matters because…
options: Latency changes the model’s accuracy
Small models use more memory per token
Users type faster than the large model responds
Large models cannot stream tokens
mcq.why: Interactive features need answers within keystrokes.
distractors: They can stream, but the first token is still slow.

mcq.q: Misrouted messages each cost 2 minutes of agent time. 10,000 extra misroutes cost about…
options: 33 hours
333 hours
20 hours
3,333 hours

mcq.q: What usually decides whether a small model is "good enough"?
options: Its parameter count compared with others
Its position on a public leaderboard
A pre-agreed metric on held-out data
How fluent its answers sound
mcq.why: Acceptance criteria are written before testing (8.1).
distractors: Size says little about task fit.

mcq.q: In distillation, the teacher is…
options: The evaluation suite used for the release gates
The smaller model that is being trained
The large model whose outputs train the student
The human who labels the held-out test set
mcq.why: The teacher produces the labels or outputs the student learns from.
distractors: Humans write the test labels, not teacher outputs.

mcq.q: Why must the test set be labelled by people, not by the teacher?
options: The teacher refuses to label test data
Otherwise you measure agreement with the teacher
The student cannot read teacher labels
People are faster than the teacher
mcq.why: Teacher-labelled tests hide the teacher’s own mistakes.

mcq.q: The teacher labels 10,000 inputs and is wrong on 12%. How many bad labels?
Asking the teacher twice and keeping only agreeing labels mainly removes…
options: Unstable answers the teacher is unsure of
Every hard example that appears in the data
Duplicate inputs that appear in the pool
Personal data contained in the inputs
mcq.why: Disagreement between samples signals uncertainty.
distractors: Some hard but stable cases remain.

mcq.q: After filtering by confidence, a rare category has only 3 examples left. The best response is…
options: Oversample rare cases before labelling, then refilter
Lower every threshold for all categories
Ignore it, since rare categories rarely matter
Copy the three examples a hundred times
mcq.why: Get more real examples of the rare category, then filter.
distractors: Lowering all thresholds adds noise everywhere.

mcq.q: Two teacher calls per input at 0.004 dollars for 10,000 inputs cost…
options: 80 dollars
8 dollars
800 dollars
40 dollars

mcq.q: A provider’s terms forbid using outputs to train competing models. Before distilling you should…
options: Check the terms and record the decision
Distil anyway since outputs are yours
Use the outputs only for evaluation
Hide which teacher was used
mcq.why: Licence review is part of data provenance (16.6).
distractors: Hiding provenance is a governance failure.

mcq.q: A human reviews 100 kept labels and finds 3 wrong. The estimated error rate of the kept set is about…
Which inputs should a teacher-data pipeline oversample?
options: Duplicates of common cases
Rare and hard real cases
Synthetic text unlike real traffic
Inputs the teacher finds easy
mcq.why: The student needs coverage where it will struggle.
distractors: Unrealistic inputs teach the wrong distribution.

mcq.q: Agreement in Hinglish is much lower than in English. The sensible action is…
options: Translate Hinglish into English first
Trust Hinglish labels like the others
Drop Hinglish from the student entirely
Add human spot-checks for Hinglish labels
mcq.why: Low agreement signals a weaker teacher there; review more.

interview.followUp: How large should that set be?

interview.followUp: How would you measure the improvement?

mcq.q: Soft targets are…
options: Answers with all of their punctuation removed
Targets that are changed at every epoch
The teacher’s full probability spread over answers
Labels that the student writes for itself
mcq.why: The student learns from the whole distribution, not only the top answer.
distractors: The student does not label itself here.

mcq.q: Raising the temperature above 1 before the softmax…
options: Makes the top answer more certain
Removes the wrong answers entirely
Flattens the probabilities, showing near misses
Changes which answer is ranked first
mcq.why: Dividing scores by a larger number shrinks gaps between them.

mcq.q: Teacher scores 6.0, 3.5, 0.5, −1.0 at temperature 4 become which scores before the softmax?
mcq.why: Each score is divided by 4.

mcq.q: You distil from a hosted API that returns only text. Which method is available?
options: Logit distillation on its probabilities
Sequence-level distillation on its outputs
Copying the teacher’s weights
Pruning the teacher model
mcq.why: Without probabilities, train on generated outputs.
distractors: Needs probabilities the API does not give.
You cannot prune a hosted model.

mcq.q: Why can soft targets reach the same accuracy with fewer examples?
options: They skip the training loop entirely
Each example carries more information
They remove the need for a test set
They make the student model larger
mcq.why: The probabilities say how wrong each wrong answer is.
distractors: You still need a test set.

mcq.q: A student is trained on a teacher’s step-by-step explanations. What must you check?
options: That the explanations are correct
That the teacher used a high temperature
That the explanations are short
That the student copies them word for word
mcq.why: A student learns wrong reasoning as easily as right.
distractors: Copying is not the goal; correctness is.

mcq.q: At temperature 1, teacher probabilities are 0.92, 0.08, 0.004, 0.001. Compared with a hard label, the student additionally learns that…
options: The last answer is the safest choice
The second answer is a plausible near miss
All four answers are equally likely
The first answer is always wrong
mcq.why: The 0.08 marks the second answer as close.

mcq.q: Hard labels lose what information compared with soft targets?
options: The order in which training examples appear
How many classes the task has in total
Which wrong answers the teacher found close
Which answer the teacher picked in the end
mcq.why: A hard label keeps only the winner.

mcq.q: With 20,000 examples, hard labels give 91% and soft targets at T = 2 give 93%. Errors per 10,000 requests fall by…
Logit distillation is easiest when…
options: The teacher is a closed API
Teacher and student share a vocabulary
The student is larger than the teacher
There are no labelled examples at all
mcq.why: Matching distributions token by token needs the same tokens.

interview.followUp: When would hard labels be enough?

interview.followUp: How would you choose it?

interview.followUp: Which would you use with a hosted teacher?

interview.followUp: How would you check traces at scale?

interview.q: How would you distil a classifier that confuses two similar classes?
interview.followUp: How do you know it worked?

interview.q: How do you know whether distillation improved on plain fine-tuning?
interview.followUp: What is a meaningful gain?

interview.followUp: Where would you spend the most effort?

interview.followUp: How do you handle teacher model updates?

mcq.q: Structured pruning removes…
options: Individual small weights only
Tokens from the vocabulary
Whole heads, neurons or layers
Examples from the training set
mcq.why: Removing whole units makes matrices smaller, so it speeds things up.

mcq.q: Why may unstructured pruning give no speed-up?
options: Hardware still multiplies the zeroed weights
It disables quantisation
It always makes the model larger
Pruned weights are restored at load time
mcq.why: Without sparse support, zeros cost the same as other numbers.

mcq.q: A 3B model in 16-bit takes 6 GB. Pruned to 2B and quantised to 4-bit at about 0.55 bytes per weight, it takes about…
options: 2.2 GB
4 GB
1.1 GB
mcq.why: 2 billion × 0.55 ≈ 1.1 GB.

mcq.q: Decode reads all weights per token. At 80 GB/s, a 1.1 GB model can produce at most about…
options: 7 tokens a second
88 tokens a second
730 tokens a second
73 tokens a second

mcq.q: After pruning, quality drops from 90% to 84%. The usual next step is…
options: Ship it, since 84% is close enough to 90%
Raise the decoding temperature at serving time
Prune more weights to recover the lost speed
Retrain briefly with the original as teacher
mcq.why: Distillation from the original recovers much of the loss.

mcq.q: A team prunes 50% of weights on a CPU server and sees no speed change. The most likely reason is…
options: The test prompts were too short
The CPU was too fast already
The pruning was unstructured
The model was quantised first
mcq.why: Scattered zeros do not shrink the computation on ordinary hardware.

mcq.q: 2:4 sparsity means…
options: Two layers out of every four layers are removed
Two of every four weights are zero in a fixed pattern
Weights are stored in two bits or in four bits
Two GPUs serve every group of four requests
mcq.why: The pattern lets supported GPUs skip half the multiplications.

mcq.q: Which suites must be rerun after compressing a model?
options: None, if accuracy looks fine
Only the task suite
Only latency benchmarks
Task, general and safety suites
mcq.why: Compression can change refusals and general skills too (13.6).

mcq.q: Pruning recovered 4 of 6 lost points after retraining. If the original was 90%, the final accuracy is…
Compared with pruning, quantisation usually gives a larger decode speed-up because…
options: It reduces the number of tokens generated
It removes whole layers from the model
It enables bigger batch sizes for free
Decoding is limited by bytes read per token
mcq.why: Fewer bytes per weight means less memory traffic (14.4).

interview.q: Compare pruning and quantisation.
interview.followUp: Which would you try first?

interview.q: Why does unstructured sparsity often not speed things up?
interview.followUp: When does it help?

interview.q: How do you recover quality after pruning?
interview.followUp: How much data does recovery need?

interview.followUp: How would you prevent this next time?

interview.q: How do you decide how far to compress?
interview.followUp: What would make you stop?

interview.followUp: What if quality fails in one language?

interview.q: Design a compression pipeline that runs for every new model release.
interview.followUp: Which step is most fragile?

interview.followUp: What is the risk?

mcq.q: Which is a main benefit of on-device inference?
options: Live data without a network
Central logging of every answer
Unlimited model size on phones
Data can stay on the user’s device
mcq.why: Privacy and offline use are key benefits.
distractors: Live data still needs the network.

mcq.q: A 3B model in 4-bit (about 1.7 GB) on a phone reading memory at 50 GB/s can decode at most about…
options: 30 tokens a second
300 tokens a second
85 tokens a second
3 tokens a second

mcq.q: Why do phones often run slower over a long conversation?
options: The model grows during use
Batteries add latency at full charge
Tokens get longer over time
They throttle when hot
mcq.why: Sustained heat forces lower clock speeds.
distractors: Token length is fixed by the tokenizer.

mcq.q: An offline itinerary assistant is asked to rebook a train. It should…
options: Invent a likely new train time
Queue the request until the phone is online
Refuse all questions while offline
Confirm the rebooking from its own knowledge
mcq.why: Actions need the live system; the device cannot make them.
distractors: It can still answer itinerary questions.
It has no live data or authority.

mcq.q: An 8B model in 16-bit is about 16 GB. On a laptop with 16 GB where apps can use half, it…
options: Fits with room to spare
Fits after the first answer
Does not fit comfortably
Fits only during the day
mcq.why: 16 GB is more than the 8 GB available.

mcq.q: Which is harder for on-device models than for server models?
options: Working with no network connection at all
Seeing and fixing failures after release
Keeping the user’s data private and local
Avoiding per-request fees from a provider
mcq.why: There is no central place to collect failures, so evaluation must happen before release.

mcq.q: A bank considers moving fraud decisions onto phones. The main objection is…
options: Fraud rules change too slowly to need servers
Decisions must be central and auditable
Phones cannot run any kind of model at all
Users prefer slower answers for money matters
mcq.why: Money decisions need central control and audit.
distractors: They change often, which is worse.

mcq.q: A model download of 1.2 GB for a mobile app mainly affects…
options: The size of the KV cache for each token
Server latency for every other user
The accuracy of the model’s answers
First-run delay and update costs
mcq.why: Large downloads slow first use and every update.
distractors: Size of download does not change accuracy.

mcq.q: A type-ahead feature needs a suggestion within 100 ms. At 60 tokens a second, the longest suggestion is about…
options: 16 tokens
0.6 tokens
6 tokens
60 tokens
mcq.why: 0.1 s × 60 = 6 tokens.

mcq.q: Which runtime format is typical for running quantised models with llama.cpp?
options: CSV
YAML
GGUF
JPEG
mcq.why: llama.cpp loads GGUF files.

mcq.q: In a model cascade, the large model handles…
options: Requests the small model is unsure about or fails
Requests in random alternation
Every request, checked by the small model
Only requests from paying customers
mcq.why: The small model goes first; the hard minority is escalated.
distractors: Random splitting is an A/B test.
Tier routing is a different design.

mcq.q: Small model 0.00002 dollars, large 0.004; 15% escalated. Cost per request is about…
options: 0.0006 dollars
0.00062 dollars
0.004 dollars
0.00002 dollars

mcq.q: Why calibrate the small model’s confidence before choosing a threshold?
options: Calibration makes the model faster
It removes the need for escalation
Raw confidences are often overconfident
Thresholds only work on calibrated text
mcq.why: A 90% score should mean 90% right before you rely on it.

mcq.q: 85% stay with the small model at 98% right; 15% go to the large model at 85% right. Overall accuracy is about…
A security ticket is classified confidently by the small model. A good cascade rule is…
options: Trust any confident small-model answer
Always escalate security tickets by rule
Drop security tickets from routing
Escalate only if the user complains
mcq.why: High-risk categories can be routed by rule regardless of confidence.
distractors: Confidence can be wrong where it matters most.

mcq.q: During a sale, the share escalated jumps from 12% to 35%. What should you watch?
options: Only the small model’s latency at the peak
The number of model versions in the registry
Cost, and whether new kinds of request appeared
Nothing, since quality is protected by escalation
mcq.why: Escalation share drives cost and signals drift.

mcq.q: Raising the threshold so 30% are escalated instead of 15% roughly…
options: Doubles the large-model cost
Removes the small-model cost
Halves the large-model cost
Leaves cost unchanged
mcq.why: Twice as many requests go to the expensive model.
distractors: Every request still pays the small model.

mcq.q: Which signal can catch a small model’s visible failure without confidence scores?
options: A schema or rule check on its answer
The time of day of the request
The user’s account age
The length of the user’s message
mcq.why: Failed checks are a direct reason to escalate.

mcq.q: A team uses one threshold for all languages, and Hinglish errors rise. A better design is…
options: Ignoring language in routing
Removing the large model from the cascade
Language-specific thresholds or rules
A higher threshold for English only
mcq.why: Route by where the small model is weak.

mcq.q: How do you pick the threshold?
options: Always 0.5, whatever the task or the model
Whatever value the model vendor recommends
From a curve of accuracy against share escalated
The highest confidence value the model reports
mcq.why: Choose the point that meets the quality bar at the lowest cost.
